Lectures 10–11 Exercise — Trees, Bagging, Random Forests and Boosting

PubH 6010 Independent Study · Replicating Lombard et al. (2021): machine-learning models of arsenic in US private wells

Katie O’Brien

2026-11-15

1 Overview

Lectures 10 and 11 cover all of the tree-based methods: classification trees with cost-complexity pruning, bagging, random forests and boosting, plus variable importance and partial dependence plots. This week’s paper uses boosting and a random forest to build a national map of arsenic in private wells. It is a direct example of ML used for exposure assessment in a health study.

Lombard MA, Scannell Bryan M, Jones DK, Bulka C, Bradley PM, Backer LC, Focazio MJ, Silverman DT, Toccalino P, Argos M, Gribble MO, Ayotte JD. Machine learning models of arsenic in private wells throughout the conterminous United States as a tool for exposure assessment in human health studies. Environmental Science & Technology. 2021;55(8):5012–5023. doi:[10.1021/acs.est.0c05239](https://doi.org/10.1021/acs.est.0c05239)

The data are a USGS data release: Lombard MA (2021), doi:[10.5066/P90RBJXS](https://doi.org/10.5066/P90RBJXS).

Reading before you start.

  • Read the Introduction and Methods, Table 1 and the variable-importance figure (Figure 2).
  • Skim the maps. The Discussion of how the maps should and should not be used in health studies is short and worth reading closely.

The paper’s four models.

model outcome method the paper’s tuned settings
BRT1 / BRT5 / BRT10 arsenic > 1, > 5, > 10 µg/L (binary) boosted regression trees (gbm) BRT10: 4,500 trees, interaction depth 6, shrinkage 0.01, min. 10 obs. per node
RFC ≤ 5, > 5 to ≤ 10, > 10 µg/L (3 classes) random forest classification 500 trees, m = 20

We focus on > 10 µg/L, the EPA maximum contaminant level (MCL) for public water systems. Private wells are not covered by the MCL. The paper selected tuning settings by 10-fold CV with the 1-SE rule, as in the slides, and evaluated on a held-out 30% of wells. The data file records which wells were in the paper’s training and test sets, so you can use exactly the paper’s split.

Code: slides vs here. As in previous weeks, we use tidymodels where the slides use caret. For the replication in Part A we call gbm() directly, because that is what the paper and slides 13–17 of Lecture 11 use.

slides here
rpart(..., method = "class", cp = 0), printcp(), plotcp(), prune() the same (Part B), plus decision_tree(cost_complexity = tune()) |> set_engine("rpart")
randomForest(..., mtry = 8), train(method = "rf") rand_forest(mtry = , trees = , min_n = 1) |> set_engine("ranger")
gbm(..., distribution = "bernoulli") the same (Part A)
train(method = "gbm", tuneGrid = expand.grid(...)) boost_tree(trees = tune(), tree_depth = tune(), learn_rate = tune()) |> set_engine("xgboost")
varImpPlot(), summary(gbm_fit), plot(gbm_fit, i = "x") the same for gbm; importance = "permutation" in ranger; pdp_curve() (starter code)
trainControl("cv", number = 10) vfold_cv(train, v = 5, strata = as10). We use 5 folds to keep the boosting grid under 5 minutes

Install once: install.packages(c("tidymodels", "gbm", "rpart.plot", "ranger", "xgboost", "probably")). rpart ships with R.

2 Data

AsModelInput.csv: 20,450 private wells sampled 1970–2013 across the conterminous US, × 93 columns. Well locations are not included. Model_input_definitions.csv defines every column, and Model_input_sources.csv gives the source datasets.

columns what they are
bas1, bas5, bas10 1 if arsenic > 1, > 5, > 10 µg/L (NA where a well’s reporting limit is too high to classify it)
As3Cat C1 ≤ 5, C2 > 5 to ≤ 10, C3 ≥ 10 µg/L
spl1, spl5, spl10, spl3cat TRUE = the paper’s training set, FALSE = test set, for each model
85 predictors climate and hydrology (DMppt8110 precipitation, PRMS8110Re recharge, BFI baseflow index, LP* hydrologic position); soil C-horizon geochemistry (as_c, se_c, sb_c, p_c, …); and 68 binary geology, surficial-material and ecoregion indicators

Three things in the definitions file are wrong or inconsistent. The starter code accounts for them:

  • DMppt8110 is listed in inches. The values (65 to 3,098) are millimetres per year.
  • The descriptions of p_c and orgc_c are swapped. p_c is phosphorus (mg/kg), and orgc_c is organic carbon (weight %).
  • C3 is “≥ 10” but bas10 is “> 10”, so wells at exactly 10 µg/L are C3 with bas10 = 0.

The starter code drops the 27 wells with a missing predictor and creates as10, a factor version of bas10 with "yes" as the first level (yardstick treats the first level as the event).

Submit your knitted .Rmd with short written answers to the questions in bold.

3 Tasks

3.1 Part A — Replicate the boosted model for > 10 µg/L (L11 slides 4–7, 13–15)

  1. Using the paper’s split (spl10), report the number of training and test wells and the proportion with arsenic > 10 µg/L in each.
library(tidyverse)
library(tidymodels)
library(gbm)
library(rpart)
library(rpart.plot)
library(ranger)
library(xgboost)
library(probably)
tidymodels_prefer()

as_raw <- read_csv("AsModelInput.csv")
outcome_cols <- c("bas1", "bas5", "bas10", "As3Cat", "spl1", "spl5", "spl10", "spl3cat")
predictors   <- setdiff(names(as_raw), outcome_cols)          # 85 predictors

wells <- as_raw |>
  filter(if_all(all_of(predictors), \(x) !is.na(x))) |>      # drops 27 wells
  mutate(as10   = factor(if_else(bas10 == 1, "yes", "no"), levels = c("yes", "no")),
         As3Cat = factor(As3Cat))
train <- wells |> filter(spl10)
test  <- wells |> filter(!spl10)
f10   <- reformulate(predictors, response = "as10")

# ---- helper: the five Table 1 metrics at a probability cutoff ----------------
test_metrics <- function(truth, prob_yes, cut = 0.5) {
  cls <- factor(if_else(prob_yes > cut, "yes", "no"), levels = c("yes", "no"))
  tibble(accuracy    = accuracy_vec(truth, cls),
         sensitivity = sensitivity_vec(truth, cls),
         specificity = specificity_vec(truth, cls),
         auc         = roc_auc_vec(truth, prob_yes),
         kappa       = kap_vec(truth, cls))
}


train %>% 
  count(bas10 == "1")
## # A tibble: 2 × 2
##   `bas10 == "1"`     n
##   <lgl>          <int>
## 1 FALSE          12759
## 2 TRUE            1544
test %>%
  count(bas10 == "1")
## # A tibble: 2 × 2
##   `bas10 == "1"`     n
##   <lgl>          <int>
## 1 FALSE           5459
## 2 TRUE             661

There are 14,303 wells in the training dataset. 1,544 of these have arsenic levels above 10 ug/L. There are 6,120 wells in the testing dataset. 661 of these wells have arsenic levels above 10 ug/L.

  1. Fit the paper’s BRT10 with gbm() (settings in the table above, bag.fraction = 0.5, set.seed(1234)). Compute test-set accuracy, sensitivity, specificity, AUC and kappa at the 0.5 cutoff, and the same on the training set, with test_metrics(). Put them next to the paper’s Table 1.
# ---- Part A ------------------------------------------------------------------
set.seed(1234)
gbm10 <- gbm(reformulate(predictors, "bas10"), data = train,   # gbm wants a 0/1 outcome
             distribution = "bernoulli", n.trees = 4500, interaction.depth = 6,
             shrinkage = 0.01, n.minobsinnode = 10, bag.fraction = 0.5)   # ~2-4 min
p_gbm_test <- predict(gbm10, test, n.trees = 4500, type = "response")
metrics <- test_metrics(test$as10, p_gbm_test)

metrics_long <- metrics %>%
  pivot_longer(
    cols = everything(),
    names_to = "metric",
    values_to = " GBMmodel"
  )

table1 <- tibble(
  metric = c("accuracy", "sensitivity", "specificity", "auc", "kappa"), 
  paper = c("91.2", "33.9", "98.2", "0.850", "0.413")
)


left_join(table1, metrics_long, by = "metric")
## # A tibble: 5 × 3
##   metric      paper ` GBMmodel`
##   <chr>       <chr>       <dbl>
## 1 accuracy    91.2        0.912
## 2 sensitivity 33.9        0.336
## 3 specificity 98.2        0.981
## 4 auc         0.850       0.856
## 5 kappa       0.413       0.409
  1. Two baselines: the accuracy of predicting “no” for every well, and a main-effects logistic regression (logistic_reg()) on all 85 predictors.
# baseline model for predicting no 
p_baseline_no <- rep(0, nrow(test))
test_metrics(test$as10, p_baseline_no)
## # A tibble: 1 × 5
##   accuracy sensitivity specificity   auc kappa
##      <dbl>       <dbl>       <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>
## 1    0.892           0           1   0.5     0
# logistic regression model
logit10 <- logistic_reg() |> fit(f10, data = train)
p_logit_test <- predict(logit10, test, type = "prob")$.pred_yes
test_metrics(test$as10, p_logit_test)
## # A tibble: 1 × 5
##   accuracy sensitivity specificity   auc kappa
##      <dbl>       <dbl>       <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>
## 1    0.901       0.129       0.995 0.795 0.194

Q1. Do your numbers match Table 1? Give two reasons small differences could remain. Why is training performance so much better than test performance, and why is this a bigger concern for boosting than for a random forest (slide 7)? Compare the model’s 91% accuracy with the “always no” baseline. Which of the five metrics would you lead with in an abstract, and why? What does interaction.depth = 6 mean in gbm?

The numbers do match table 1 for the most part, with some small differences. Small differences could remain because the models uses a stochastic process, which is random, and the samples chosen in the subsampling step may be different every time. Training performance is better than test performance because the model is using data it has seen before. This is a bigger concern for boosting than for random forest because, in boosting, decisions are made based on the previous tree, so the order the trees were created in is important. The accuracy of the “always no” model is 89%. I would lead with accuracy in the metric because it describes the ratio of correct predictions to total predictions, which would be helpful for this topic. In GBM, interaction.depth specifies the maximum number of splits to perform on each individual tree.

3.2 Part B — A single classification tree (L10 slides 25–37)

  1. Grow the maximal tree with rpart(..., cp = 0, xval = 10) (slide 31). Use plotcp() and the cptable to find the α with the smallest CV error and the α chosen by the 1-SE rule.
set.seed(1234)
tree_max <- rpart(f10, data = train, method = "class", parms = list(split = "gini"),
                  control = rpart.control(minsplit = 20, minbucket = 5, cp = 0, xval = 10))
printcp(tree_max)

The alpha with the smallest cp value is 0.0019. Within 1-SE, the alpha value is 0.006.

  1. Tune cost_complexity with tidymodels on the 5 folds, with both accuracy and roc_auc as metrics. Plot both against α. Report the test metrics of the tree chosen by the 1-SE rule on accuracy and of the tree with the best CV AUC.
set.seed(1234)
folds <- vfold_cv(train, v = 5, strata = as10)            # reuse these folds in Part D
cart_spec <- decision_tree(cost_complexity = tune(), min_n = 20) |>
  set_engine("rpart") |> set_mode("classification")
cart_res <- tune_grid(workflow(f10, cart_spec), resamples = folds,
                      grid = tibble(cost_complexity = 10^seq(-4, -1.5, by = 0.5)),
                      metrics = metric_set(accuracy, roc_auc))
# model chosen by 1 SE rule using accuracy
hp_1se_acc <- select_by_one_std_err(cart_res, desc(cost_complexity), metric = "accuracy")

# plotting accuracy and ROC against alpha
autoplot(cart_res) +
  scale_x_log10() +
  labs(
    x = "Alpha",
    y = "CV Metric",
    title = "Decision Tree Tuning Performance"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

hp_best_auc <- select_best(
  cart_res, 
  metric = "roc_auc"
)

cart_wf <- workflow(f10, cart_spec)

# helper function for test metrics
get_model_test_metrics <- function(hp_selected, model_label) {
  final_wf <- finalize_workflow(cart_wf, hp_selected)
  fit_model <- fit(final_wf, data = train)
  
  # Predict test probabilities for the positive class ("yes")
  test_probs <- predict(fit_model, new_data = test, type = "prob")$.pred_yes
  
  # Calculate test metrics using your custom helper function
  test_metrics(truth = test$as10, prob_yes = test_probs, cut = 0.5) %>%
    mutate(model = model_label, .before = 1)
}

# metrics for models chosen by 1 SE accuracy and CV AUC
results_1se_acc  <- get_model_test_metrics(hp_1se_acc, "1-SE Rule (Accuracy)")
results_best_auc <- get_model_test_metrics(hp_best_auc, "Best CV AUC")

combined_test_metrics <- bind_rows(results_1se_acc, results_best_auc)

print(combined_test_metrics)

  1. Prune to a small tree (cp = 0.0065, 3 splits) and draw it with rpart.plot(). Then grow the same small tree on three bootstrap resamples of the training wells (slice_sample(train, prop = 1, replace = TRUE)) and record the first few splits of each.
# prune to a small tree
tree_small <- rpart::prune(tree_max, cp = 0.0065)   # rpart::, because another package also has a prune()
rpart.plot(tree_small, extra = 107)

tree_formula <- formula(tree_max)
tree_control <- tree_max$control

# Set seed for reproducibility across bootstrap samples
set.seed(123)

# bootstrap samples
for (i in 1:3) {
  
  # resample with replacement
  boot_train <- slice_sample(train, prop = 1, replace = TRUE)
  
  # fit tree and prune
  boot_tree_max <- rpart(tree_formula, data = boot_train, control = tree_control)
  boot_tree_small <- rpart::prune(boot_tree_max, cp = 0.0065)
  
  # show first few splits
  print(boot_tree_small)
}

Q2. Describe the small tree in two sentences a state health department could use. Why do accuracy and AUC choose such different trees (think about the 89% baseline and slide 30)? How does the best single tree compare with the boosted model and with logistic regression? What did the bootstrap resamples show, and how does it connect to the motivation for bagging (slides 37–40)? Hint: compute the correlation between as_c and sb_c.

This tree identifies important predictors of wells contaminated with private arsenic. Important predictors include precipitation, soil C-horizon geochemistry, and organic carbon. Accuracy and AUC choose different trees because accuracy is based on the ratio of correct predictions to total predictions while AUC is based on on the true positive rate vs the false positive rate. The best model (using the tree within 1 SE of the best accuracy) has similar accuracy to the boosted model and logistic regression, a sensitivity value and kappa value in between them, and has slightly lower specificity and AUC. The bootstrap resamples showed that precipitation is the root split of every tree. This connects to the motivation for bagging because bagging reduces the variance of prediction models.

3.3 Part C — Bagging and random forests (L10 slides 38–53)

  1. With rf_fit() (starter code), fit bagging (m = 85) and a random forest (m = 9 ≈ √85) for B ∈ {10, 25, 50, 100, 250, 500, 1000}. Plot the OOB error against B for both (slide 44).
# starter code
# min_n = 1 grows full trees, as randomForest() does (slides 41, 52)
rf_fit <- function(mtry, trees = 500, data = train, formula = f10, ...) {
  rand_forest(mtry = mtry, trees = trees, min_n = 1) |>
    set_engine("ranger", seed = 1234, ...) |>
    set_mode("classification") |>
    fit(formula, data = data)
}
rf20 <- rf_fit(20)
extract_fit_engine(rf20)$prediction.error                 # OOB Brier score
## [1] 0.06621888
oob_prob <- extract_fit_engine(rf20)$predictions[, "yes"] # OOB probability for every training well
roc_auc_vec(train$as10, oob_prob)                         # OOB AUC
## [1] 0.8642034
# 3-class: rf_fit(20, data = train3, formula = reformulate(predictors, "As3Cat"))
#   with train3 <- wells |> filter(!is.na(As3Cat), spl3cat)



# B grid
B_grid <- c(10, 25, 50, 100, 250, 500, 1000)

# function to extract OOB error
get_oob_error <- function(mtry, trees) {
  fit_obj <- rf_fit(mtry = mtry, trees = trees)
  extract_fit_engine(fit_obj)$prediction.error
}

# grid search across B for bagging (m = 85) and random forest (m = 9)
q7_results <- expand.grid(
  trees = B_grid,
  model = c("Bagging (m = 85)", "Random Forest (m = 9)")
) %>%
  mutate(
    mtry = if_else(model == "Bagging (m = 85)", 85, 9),
    oob_error = map2_dbl(mtry, trees, get_oob_error)
  )

# plotting OOB error aginast B values
ggplot(q7_results, aes(x = trees, y = oob_error, color = model, group = model)) +
  geom_line(size = 1) +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  scale_x_log10(breaks = B_grid) +
  labs(
    x = "Number of Trees (B)",
    y = "OOB Brier Score (Prediction Error)",
    title = "OOB Error vs. Number of Trees (B)",
    color = "Model Type"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

  1. With B = 500, fit m ∈ {1, 3, 6, 9, 15, 20, 30, 45, 60, 85}. Tabulate the OOB Brier score and OOB AUC against m. Report the test metrics for bagging, m = 9 and the paper’s m = 20.
# M grid
m_grid <- c(1, 3, 6, 9, 15, 20, 30, 45, 60, 85)

# function to get OOB error
get_oob_metrics <- function(mtry) {
  fit_obj <- rf_fit(mtry = mtry, trees = 500)
  engine <- extract_fit_engine(fit_obj)
  
  brier <- engine$prediction.error
  oob_prob <- engine$predictions[, "yes"]
  auc <- roc_auc_vec(train$as10, oob_prob)
  
  tibble(m = mtry, oob_brier = brier, oob_auc = auc)
}

#calculate OOB brier and OOB AUC
q8_oob_table <- map_dfr(m_grid, get_oob_metrics)
print("OOB Brier and OOB AUC Table:")
## [1] "OOB Brier and OOB AUC Table:"
print(q8_oob_table)

##  3     6    0.0654   0.871
##  4     9    0.0653   0.869
##  5    15    0.0661   0.864
##  6    20    0.0662   0.864
##  7    30    0.0669   0.859
##  8    45    0.0672   0.858
##  9    60    0.0675   0.857
## 10    85    0.0681   0.857
# helper to evaluate performance
eval_rf_test <- function(mtry, label) {
  fit_obj <- rf_fit(mtry = mtry, trees = 500)
  
  # predict test probabilities for positive class "yes"
  test_prob <- predict(fit_obj, new_data = test, type = "prob")$.pred_yes
  
  test_metrics(truth = test$as10, prob_yes = test_prob, cut = 0.5) %>%
    mutate(model = label, m = mtry, .before = 1)
}

# test metrics for Bagging (m = 85), m = 9, and m = 20
test_bagging <- eval_rf_test(85, "Bagging (m = 85)")
test_m9      <- eval_rf_test(9,  "Random Forest (m = 9)")
test_m20     <- eval_rf_test(20, "Paper's RF (m = 20)")

q8_test_metrics <- bind_rows(test_bagging, test_m9, test_m20)
print(q8_test_metrics)

  1. Replicate the paper’s 3-class RFC on its split (spl3cat, m = 20, 500 trees). Report accuracy on the training data, OOB accuracy, test accuracy and test kappa, and the accuracy of always predicting C1. Make the test confusion matrix and compute the precision and recall of each class.
#  3-class training and testing datasets
train3 <- wells %>% filter(!is.na(As3Cat), spl3cat)
test3  <- wells %>% filter(!is.na(As3Cat), !spl3cat)

# extract predictor variable names from f10
predictors <- all.vars(f10[[3]])
f3cat <- reformulate(predictors, "As3Cat")

# 3-class Random Forest model
rf3_fit <- rf_fit(mtry = 20, trees = 500, data = train3, formula = f3cat)
rf3_engine <- extract_fit_engine(rf3_fit)

# training accuracy and kappa
train3_preds <- predict(rf3_fit, new_data = train3)$.pred_class
train_acc <- accuracy_vec(train3$As3Cat, train3_preds)

# OOB accuracy
oob_acc <- 1 - rf3_engine$prediction.error

# test accuracy and kappa
test3_preds <- predict(rf3_fit, new_data = test3)$.pred_class
test_acc   <- accuracy_vec(test3$As3Cat, test3_preds)
test_kappa <- kap_vec(test3$As3Cat, test3_preds)

# baseline accuracy
baseline_acc <- mean(test3$As3Cat == "C1")

# test confusion matrix
test3_df <- tibble(
  truth = test3$As3Cat,
  estimate = test3_preds
)

conf_mat_3class <- conf_mat(test3_df, truth = truth, estimate = estimate)
print(conf_mat_3class)
##           Truth
## Prediction   C1   C2   C3
##         C1 4508  371  333
##         C2   64   61   57
##         C3  121   66  323
# per-class precision and recall
cm <- conf_mat_3class$table
precision <- diag(cm) / rowSums(cm)
recall <- diag(cm) / colSums(cm)

per_class_metrics <- tibble(
  class = colnames(cm), 
  precision = precision, 
  recall = recall
)

print(per_class_metrics)

Q3. How many trees are enough, and can too many trees hurt here (slide 51)? Which m is best, and why does bagging do worse than a random forest on these predictors (slide 50)? The paper reports 100% training accuracy for the RFC. Is that evidence of overfitting, and which of your numbers is the honest estimate of performance on new wells? Why is C2 (5–10 µg/L) so hard to predict, and why does that matter for a health study? Finally, compare your per-class precision and recall with the paper’s “user’s” and “producer’s” accuracy (look up the definitions). What do you notice?

About 250 trees are enough based on the OOB error. There is no risk of overfitting by using more trees. m = 9 is best based on the OOB error. Bagging does worse than random forest on these predictors because the predictors are highly correlated. 100% training accuracy for the RFC is evidence of overfitting. The honest estimate of performance on new wells is 83% accuracy. C2 is hard to predict because there are fewer wells that fit into this category in the training dataset. This matters for a health study because accurately predicting contaminated wells is important for employing appropriate interventions.

3.4 Part D — Tuning boosted trees with tidymodels (L11 slides 7, 18–21)

  1. Tune boost_tree() with the xgboost engine (min_n = 10, sample_size = 0.5) over trees ∈ {250, 500, 1000, 2000, 3000} × tree_depth ∈ {1, 3, 6} × learn_rate ∈ {0.01, 0.1}, using CV AUC. Plot CV AUC against trees, coloured by depth and faceted by learning rate.
xgb_spec <- boost_tree(trees = tune(), tree_depth = tune(), learn_rate = tune(),
                       min_n = 10, sample_size = 0.5) |>
  set_engine("xgboost") |> set_mode("classification")
xgb_grid <- expand_grid(trees = c(250, 500, 1000, 2000, 3000),
                        tree_depth = c(1, 3, 6), learn_rate = c(0.01, 0.1))
xgb_res <- tune_grid(workflow(f10, xgb_spec), resamples = folds, grid = xgb_grid,
                     metrics = metric_set(roc_auc, accuracy))     # ~2-5 min

# metrics
xgb_auc_df <- collect_metrics(xgb_res) |>
  filter(.metric == "roc_auc") |>
  mutate(
    tree_depth = factor(tree_depth),
    learn_rate_label = paste("Learning Rate:", learn_rate)
  )

# plot CV AUC against trees, colored by depth and faceted by learning
ggplot(xgb_auc_df, aes(x = trees, y = mean, color = tree_depth, group = tree_depth)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  facet_wrap(~ learn_rate_label) +
  labs(
    x = "Number of Trees",
    y = "Cross-Validation Mean AUC",
    color = "Tree Depth",
    title = "XGBoost Hyperparameter Tuning Performance (CV AUC)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

Q4. What happens to CV AUC as B grows at ν = 0.1 vs ν = 0.01, and why? What do depth-1 trees (stumps) assume, and what does their gap from depth 6 tell you about interactions in arsenic geochemistry? Is xgboost’s tree_depth = 6 the same as gbm’s interaction.depth = 6? In your final table, which differences are large and which are within noise? (A rough SE for a test AUC here is 0.008.)

At v = 0.01, CV AUC increases as tree depth increases. At 0.1, CV AUC increases from a tree depth of 1 vs tree depths of 3 vs 6, but AUC is relatively the same at tree depths of 3 vs 6. This is because at a slower learning rate, the model is more likely to not miss the minimum for the loss function. Depth-1 trees assume that there are no interactions between features. Their gap from depth-6 trees implies that there are interactions in arsenic geochemistry. Tree_depth in xgboost is not quite same thing as interaction.depth in gbm, but they are related. In the final table, there are large differences between sensitivity and kappa. There are also differences in AUC. In AUC, the differences between bagging, random forest, the paper’s GBM, and the tuned xgboost are all within noise (because they are within 1 SE of each other), but the differences bewteen logistic regression and best CART are large differences.

  map_dfr(grid, \(v) tibble(value = v, yhat = mean(pred_fun(mutate(data, !!var := v)))))
}

# GBM partial dependence curve
pdp_gbm <- pdp_curve(
  \(nd) predict(gbm10, nd, n.trees = 4500, type = "response"), 
  pdp_sample, 
  "DMppt8110"
) %>%
  mutate(model = "GBM")

# random forest partial dependence curve
pdp_rf <- pdp_curve(
  \(nd) predict(rf20, nd, type = "prob")$.pred_yes, 
  pdp_sample, 
  "DMppt8110"
) %>%
  mutate(model = "Random Forest (m=20)")

# combine curves
pdp_models <- bind_rows(pdp_gbm, pdp_rf)

#  mean precipitation and observed proportion of positive outcomes 
decile_data <- train %>%
  filter(!is.na(DMppt8110), !is.na(as10)) %>%
  mutate(decile = ntile(DMppt8110, 10)) %>%
  group_by(decile) %>%
  summarise(
    value = mean(DMppt8110),
    yhat = mean(as10 == "yes"),
    model = "Observed Decile Prop.",
    .groups = "drop"
  )

# plot
ggplot() +
  # Model Partial Dependence Lines
  geom_line(
    data = pdp_models, 
    aes(x = value, y = yhat, color = model), 
    linewidth = 1.1, linetype = "solid"
  ) +
  geom_line(
    data = decile_data, 
    aes(x = value, y = yhat, color = model), 
    linetype = "solid", 
    linewidth = 0.8
  ) +
  scale_color_manual(
    name = "Legend",
    values = c(
      "GBM" = "lightblue", 
      "Random Forest (m=20)" = "darkseagreen3", 
      "Observed Decile Prop." = "orchid"
    )
  ) +
  labs(
    x = "Precipitation",
    y = "Predicted Probability / Proportion > 10 µg/L",
    title = "Partial Dependence Plot for Precipitation",
    color = "Legend",
    linetype = "Legend"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

  1. Using the random forest’s OOB predicted probabilities (no test data), plot sensitivity, specificity and PPV against the cutoff with probably::threshold_perf(). Pick the cutoff that maximises Youden’s J. Apply it to the test set and report sensitivity, specificity, PPV and the share of wells flagged.
# oob_df <- tibble(truth = train$as10, .pred_yes = oob_prob) |>
  # threshold_perf(truth, .pred_yes, thresholds = seq(0.02, 0.6, by = 0.01),
               # metrics = metric_set(sensitivity, specificity, j_index, ppv))

oob_prob <- extract_fit_engine(rf20)$predictions[, "yes"]

oob_df <- tibble(
  truth    = train$as10, 
  .pred_yes = oob_prob
)

thresh_perf <- oob_df |>
  threshold_perf(
    truth, 
    .pred_yes, 
    thresholds = seq(0.02, 0.6, by = 0.01),
    metrics    = metric_set(sensitivity, specificity, j_index, ppv)
  )

# calculate sensitivity and specificity
thresh_perf %>%
  filter(.metric %in% c("sens", "spec", "ppv")) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = .threshold, y = .estimate, color = .metric)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  labs(
    x = "Probability Threshold (Cutoff)",
    y = "Metric Value",
    title = "Random Forest OOB Performance across Decision Cutoffs",
    color = "Metric"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

# find cutoff value
best_cutoff_row <- thresh_perf %>%
  filter(.metric == "j_index") %>%
  slice_max(.estimate, n = 1, with_ties = FALSE)

best_cutoff <- best_cutoff_row$.threshold
print(best_cutoff)
## [1] 0.13
# apply best cutoff to metrics
# predict test set probabilities using rf20
test_prob_rf20 <- predict(rf20, new_data = test, type = "prob")$.pred_yes

test_perf_optimal <- test_metrics(
  truth = test$as10, 
  prob_yes = test_prob_rf20, 
  cut = best_cutoff
) %>%
  mutate(
    cutoff = best_cutoff,
    share_flagged = mean(test_prob_rf20 > best_cutoff),
    .before = 1
  )

print(test_perf_optimal)
## # A tibble: 1 × 7
##   cutoff share_flagged accuracy sensitivity specificity   auc kappa
##    <dbl>         <dbl>    <dbl>       <dbl>       <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>
## 1   0.13         0.238    0.810       0.723       0.821 0.856 0.356

Q5. Which predictors are important under all three measures, and where do the measures disagree? Why might impurity importance favour continuous variables over rare binary ones? Describe the precipitation partial dependence, and say whether it is a causal effect of precipitation. Is it relevant to your extreme-weather question? (Precipitation here is a 1981–2010 average.) If an epidemiologist used these predictions as the exposure in a study of arsenic and bladder cancer, would you give them the 0.5 class, your Youden class, or the probability, and why? Last, the paper’s test set is a random 30% of wells. What would a spatially blocked test set measure that this one does not?

Precipitation and soil horizon geochemistry variables are important under all three measures. Impurity importance may favor continuous variables over rare binary ones because there is more opportunity for splitting. The partial dependence plot for precipitation shows that there is a large influence of precipitation in the models, but it is unclear if it is a causal effect of precipitation. If an epidemiologist used these predictions as the exposure in a study of arsenic and bladder cancer, I would give them the probability. A spatially blocked test set would consider how far away training and testing well points are.

4 Starter code

library(tidyverse)
library(tidymodels)
library(gbm)
library(rpart)
library(rpart.plot)
library(ranger)
library(xgboost)
library(probably)
tidymodels_prefer()

as_raw <- read_csv("AsModelInput.csv")
outcome_cols <- c("bas1", "bas5", "bas10", "As3Cat", "spl1", "spl5", "spl10", "spl3cat")
predictors   <- setdiff(names(as_raw), outcome_cols)          # 85 predictors

wells <- as_raw |>
  filter(if_all(all_of(predictors), \(x) !is.na(x))) |>      # drops 27 wells
  mutate(as10   = factor(if_else(bas10 == 1, "yes", "no"), levels = c("yes", "no")),
         As3Cat = factor(As3Cat))
train <- wells |> filter(spl10)
test  <- wells |> filter(!spl10)
f10   <- reformulate(predictors, response = "as10")

# ---- helper: the five Table 1 metrics at a probability cutoff ----------------
test_metrics <- function(truth, prob_yes, cut = 0.5) {
  cls <- factor(if_else(prob_yes > cut, "yes", "no"), levels = c("yes", "no"))
  tibble(accuracy    = accuracy_vec(truth, cls),
         sensitivity = sensitivity_vec(truth, cls),
         specificity = specificity_vec(truth, cls),
         auc         = roc_auc_vec(truth, prob_yes),
         kappa       = kap_vec(truth, cls))
}

# ---- Part A ------------------------------------------------------------------
set.seed(1234)
gbm10 <- gbm(reformulate(predictors, "bas10"), data = train,   # gbm wants a 0/1 outcome
             distribution = "bernoulli", n.trees = 4500, interaction.depth = 6,
             shrinkage = 0.01, n.minobsinnode = 10, bag.fraction = 0.5)   # ~2-4 min
p_gbm_test <- predict(gbm10, test, n.trees = 4500, type = "response")
test_metrics(test$as10, p_gbm_test)

logit10 <- logistic_reg() |> fit(f10, data = train)
p_logit_test <- predict(logit10, test, type = "prob")$.pred_yes

# ---- Part B ------------------------------------------------------------------
set.seed(1234)
tree_max <- rpart(f10, data = train, method = "class", parms = list(split = "gini"),
                  control = rpart.control(minsplit = 20, minbucket = 5, cp = 0, xval = 10))
printcp(tree_max); plotcp(tree_max)

set.seed(1234)
folds <- vfold_cv(train, v = 5, strata = as10)            # reuse these folds in Part D
cart_spec <- decision_tree(cost_complexity = tune(), min_n = 20) |>
  set_engine("rpart") |> set_mode("classification")
cart_res <- tune_grid(workflow(f10, cart_spec), resamples = folds,
                      grid = tibble(cost_complexity = 10^seq(-4, -1.5, by = 0.5)),
                      metrics = metric_set(accuracy, roc_auc))
select_by_one_std_err(cart_res, desc(cost_complexity), metric = "accuracy")
tree_small <- rpart::prune(tree_max, cp = 0.0065)   # rpart::, because another package also has a prune()
rpart.plot(tree_small, extra = 107)

# ---- Part C ------------------------------------------------------------------
# min_n = 1 grows full trees, as randomForest() does (slides 41, 52)
rf_fit <- function(mtry, trees = 500, data = train, formula = f10, ...) {
  rand_forest(mtry = mtry, trees = trees, min_n = 1) |>
    set_engine("ranger", seed = 1234, ...) |>
    set_mode("classification") |>
    fit(formula, data = data)
}
rf20 <- rf_fit(20)
extract_fit_engine(rf20)$prediction.error                 # OOB Brier score
oob_prob <- extract_fit_engine(rf20)$predictions[, "yes"] # OOB probability for every training well
roc_auc_vec(train$as10, oob_prob)                         # OOB AUC
# 3-class: rf_fit(20, data = train3, formula = reformulate(predictors, "As3Cat"))
#   with train3 <- wells |> filter(!is.na(As3Cat), spl3cat)

# ---- Part D ------------------------------------------------------------------
xgb_spec <- boost_tree(trees = tune(), tree_depth = tune(), learn_rate = tune(),
                       min_n = 10, sample_size = 0.5) |>
  set_engine("xgboost") |> set_mode("classification")
xgb_grid <- expand_grid(trees = c(250, 500, 1000, 2000, 3000),
                        tree_depth = c(1, 3, 6), learn_rate = c(0.01, 0.1))
xgb_res <- tune_grid(workflow(f10, xgb_spec), resamples = folds, grid = xgb_grid,
                     metrics = metric_set(roc_auc, accuracy))     # ~2-5 min
xgb_final <- finalize_workflow(workflow(f10, xgb_spec), select_best(xgb_res, metric = "roc_auc")) |>
  last_fit(split = make_splits(train, test))
p_xgb_test <- collect_predictions(xgb_final)$.pred_yes

# ---- Part E ------------------------------------------------------------------
summary(gbm10, plotit = FALSE)                                    # relative influence
rf_perm <- rf_fit(20, importance = "permutation")
extract_fit_engine(rf_perm)$variable.importance

# partial dependence: average prediction when every well is set to each grid value (L11 slide 9)
pdp_curve <- function(pred_fun, data, var,
                      grid = quantile(data[[var]], seq(0.02, 0.98, length.out = 20))) {
  map_dfr(grid, \(v) tibble(value = v, yhat = mean(pred_fun(mutate(data, !!var := v)))))
}
set.seed(1)
pdp_sample <- slice_sample(train, n = 2000)          # 2,000 wells is plenty and much faster
pdp_curve(\(nd) predict(gbm10, nd, n.trees = 4500, type = "response"), pdp_sample, "DMppt8110")
pdp_curve(\(nd) predict(rf20, nd, type = "prob")$.pred_yes,           pdp_sample, "DMppt8110")

tibble(truth = train$as10, .pred_yes = oob_prob) |>
  threshold_perf(truth, .pred_yes, thresholds = seq(0.02, 0.6, by = 0.01),
                 metrics = metric_set(sensitivity, specificity, j_index, ppv))

5 Check your numbers

  • Part A: 14,303 training and 6,120 test wells; 10.8% exceed 10 µg/L in each. BRT10 test accuracy ≈ 0.91, sensitivity ≈ 0.34, AUC ≈ 0.85, the same as Table 1 to within 0.01. “Always no” scores 0.892.
  • Part B: the root split of every tree is on precipitation (DMppt8110 ≈ 408 mm). The small tree has 4 leaves.
  • Part C: the OOB error is flat after about 250 trees. The 3-class random forest has test accuracy ≈ 0.83 and kappa ≈ 0.40, and C2 recall is close to 0.1.
  • Part D: the best CV AUC is ≈ 0.855, at depth 6 with learning rate 0.01.
  • Runtime: about 15 minutes for everything on a laptop. Most of it is the gbm() fit in Part A (~4 min) and the two tune_grid() calls (~3 min each). Save fitted models with saveRDS() so you only fit them once.
